records.themeTitle: One’s own effort and the gift beyond it
records.themeSummary: Yosef values the holiness gained through his own struggle, even while the holiness bestowed from above is greater.
records.originHebrew: וּבְוַדַּאי הַקְּדוּשָּׁה שֶׁזָּכָה מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ הוּא יוֹתֵר מִקְּדוּשָּׁה שֶׁקָּנָה בַּעֲמָלוֹ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא לט.) אָדָם מְקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ מְעַט מְקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתוֹ הַרְבֵּה. שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ מוּכָן וְרוֹצֶה לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ קְדוּשָּׁה לַמּוּכָנִים לְקַבֵּל. וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יוֹסֵף מִצִּידוֹ הָיָה חָבִיב עָלָיו בְּחִינַת מְנַשֶּׁה עַל שֵׁם כִּי נַשַּׁנִי וְגוֹמֵר מִפְּנֵי שֶׁזֶּה זָכָה בַּעֲמָלוֹ וּבִיגִיעוֹ וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא לח.) אָדָם רוֹצֶה בְּקַב שֶׁלּוֹ מִתִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ. שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִתִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר מֵעֲשָׂרָה קַבִּין לִתְפּוֹס מִסְפָּר שָׁלֵם לְגוּזְמָא כַּנָּהוּג. אַךְ בָּא לְרַמֵּז שֶׁהָאָדָם רוֹצֶה בְּקַב שֶׁלּוֹ דְּהַיְינוּ מִדָּה אַחֲרוֹנָה קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם אִיהִי יִרְאָה כּוּלֵּי שֶׁהָאָדָם מְבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁמַּשְׁפִּיעַ לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ מִכָּל הַט׳ מִדּוֹת עַד כֶּתֶר עֶלְיוֹן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעֲמָלוֹ וִיגִיעָתוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Certainly, the holiness he received from God exceeded the holiness he acquired through his toil. As the Sages said (Yoma 39a), “A person sanctifies himself a little, and he is sanctified greatly from above.” For God is ready and desires to bestow holiness upon those prepared to receive it. Nevertheless, from Yosef’s own perspective, the aspect represented by Menashe was dear to him, expressed by “For He has made me forget,” and so forth, because this he attained through his own toil and exertion. This follows the saying (Bava Metzia 38a), “A person prefers one kav of his own to nine kav of another’s.” They said “to nine kav,” although the expression should seemingly have been “to ten kav,” using a round number for emphasis, as is customary. Rather, this hints that a person prefers his own kav—the final divine attribute, accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, which is awe … A person prefers refining himself in the quality of awe to what God bestows upon him from all the other nine attributes, up to the supernal Crown, because the latter does not come through his own toil and exertion.
records.targetHebrew: ועל זאת המדרגה העשירית רמזו ז"ל בגמ' רוצה אדם בקב שלו יותר מתשעה קבין של חבירו וקב שלו היינו המדריגה העשירית שיש לו להאדם בה כל הבחירה וזאת נקרא מעשר וע"י שמוסר אדם בחזרה זאת המדריגה העשירות הנקרא מעשר שהוא הקב שלו מנחיל לו השי"ת כל התשעה קבין הנשארים כמאמרם ז"ל בגמ' משולחן גבוה קא זכי בהו ועל זה אמרו ז"ל בגמ' (שם) עשר בשביל שתתעשר וכמבואר שם מי שרי לנסויי לקב"ה וכו' אמר לו אין חוץ מזו שנאמר ובחנוני נא בזאת וגו' היינו כי מאחר שזה האדם יכול למסור בחזרה אף הקב שלו שכבר יש בתפיסתו לכן מאמין אותו השי"ת להניח אצלו כל הטובות שבעולם כי על כל כסף וזהב שבעולם נאמר לי הכסף ולי הזהב אמר ה'
records.targetEnglish: Concerning this tenth level the Sages alluded in the Gemara: “A person prefers one kav of his own to nine kav of another’s.” “His own kav” is the tenth level in which the person possesses the sphere of choice, and this is called a tithe. By returning to God this tenth level, called the tithe—his own kav—God grants him all the nine remaining measures, as the Sages said: “He acquires them from the table on high.” Concerning this the Sages said, “Tithe so that you may become wealthy.” As explained there: “Is it permitted to test the Holy One, blessed be He?” He answered, “Yes—this is the exception, as it says, ‘Test Me, please, with this.’” Since this person can return even his own kav, already within his grasp, God trusts him to hold all the good things in the world; for concerning all the silver and gold in the world it says, “Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says Hashem.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim uses the same one-to-nine image to explain what can follow the preference for one’s own labor: the person can return even that apparently personal acquisition to God. This supplies a concrete model for the movement from Yosef’s cherished effort to Yaakov’s recognition that even the effort is sustained by God. Its tithe discussion explains the spiritual model; it does not replace Rav Tzadok’s account of the two brothers with a new calendar or legal claim.

records.themeTitle: The holiness we prepare is also received
records.themeSummary: Shabbat’s fixed holiness and the New Moon established by Israel express the divine gift and the person’s cherished participation.
records.originHebrew: וּבֶאֱמֶת לִכְאוֹרָה נִרְאֶה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהַקְדִּים קְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת שֶׁהִיא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לָדַעַת כִּי אֲנִי הַשֵּׁם מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם וְהִיא קְדוּשָּׁה דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיְּימָא מִו׳ יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קְדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא דְּקָבְעִי לֵיהּ. אָמְנָם בַּגְּמָרָא (זְבָחִים צא.) חָשִׁיב לְמוּסְפֵי רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ מְקוּדָּשׁ נֶגֶד מוּסְפֵי שַׁבָּת וְכָתַב רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי הַטַּעַם דִּמְקוּדָּשִׁין מִשֶּׁל שַׁבָּת דְּאִיקְרֵי מוֹעֵד וְאֵינוֹ מוּבָן וְכִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ נִקְרָא מוֹעֵד יְהֵא מְקוּדָּשׁ יוֹתֵר מִשַּׁבָּת שֶׁקִּדְּשׁוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ וְנִקְרָא שַׁבָּת. אַךְ לְפִי הָאָמוּר מוּבָן שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת מְעוּלָּה יוֹתֵר מִקְּדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ וְלָכֵן כָּתוּב וּבְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת יִפָּתֵחַ וּבְיוֹם הַחוֹדֶשׁ יִפָּתֵחַ דְּשָׁם מְדַבֵּר מִמַּה שֶּׁיִּפְתַּח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ. וּבְוַדַּאי קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיְּימָא קוֹדֶמֶת לִקְדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ. אָכֵן מִצַּד יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ חֲבִיבָה לָהֶן מִפְּנֵי דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי לֵיהּ וְאָדָם רוֹצֶה בְּקַב שֶׁלּוֹ וְכוּלֵּי. וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁמְּדַבֵּר מִצַּד יִשְׂרָאֵל יָבֹא כָל בָּשָׂר לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹת וְגוֹמֵר וְכֵן לְעִנְיַן קַבָּלַת פְּנֵי רַבּוֹ שֶׁבַּשּׁוּנַמִּית הִקְדִּים הַכָּתוּב חוֹדֶשׁ לְשַׁבָּת שֶׁקְּדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ חָבִיב וּמְקוּדָּשׁ יוֹתֵר מִצַּד יִשְׂרָאֵל מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּא מִצִּדָּם וְנִקְרְאוּ כְּעֵין קַב שֶׁלּוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Indeed, it would initially seem that Shabbat’s holiness should have precedence, since it comes from God, as it says, “To know that I, Hashem, sanctify you.” Its holiness has been fixed and enduring since the six days of Creation, whereas the New Moon’s holiness is established by Israel. Nevertheless, the Gemara (Zevachim 91a) regards the New Moon’s additional offerings as more sacred than Shabbat’s additional offerings. Rashi explains that they are more sacred than Shabbat’s because the New Moon is called a mo‘ed, an appointed season. This is difficult to understand: does being called an appointed season make the New Moon more sacred than Shabbat, which God sanctified and named Shabbat? What we have said explains this: from God’s side, Shabbat’s holiness certainly surpasses that of the New Moon. Therefore it says, “On Shabbat it shall be opened, and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened,” because that passage concerns what God will open. Shabbat’s fixed and enduring holiness certainly precedes the holiness of the New Moon. From Israel’s side, however, the New Moon’s holiness is dear to them because Israel sanctifies it, and “a person prefers his own kav,” and so forth. Thus, when Scripture speaks from Israel’s side—“All flesh shall come to bow down,” and so forth— and likewise in the Shunammite woman’s case concerning visiting one’s teacher, Scripture places the New Moon before Shabbat. The New Moon’s holiness is dearer and more sacred from Israel’s perspective because it comes through them, and is thus regarded as akin to “his own kav.”
records.targetHebrew: היינו שבאמת מהיכן ניקח כח לישראל לקדש את המועדות וראשי חדשים, הוא הכל יען אשר יש בו קדושת שבת שהוא קבוע וקיימא, כדאיתא בזוה"ק (תרומה קלה.) אנן נטלין מתורה שבכתב תורה שבעל פה וכו' וכן מקדושת שבת קדושת יו"ט. וזה שאמר בחד בשבא איקבע ירחא, היינו שתיכף ומיד אחר השבת איקבע ירחא, שלא היה שום הפסקה מן קדושת שבת לקדושת ר"ח, כדי שיהיה להם הכרה, כי כל קדושתם והכנתם אשר יש להם הוא הכל נמשך מקדושת שבת. וחד אמר בתרי בשבא איקבע ירחא, היינו שבאמצע היה הפסקה מיום אחד דחול, היינו שנסתר מהם זה האור מקדושת שבת ונדמה להם שיש להם כח פעולה, ואח"כ בקעו את זה ההסתר והיה להם הכנה על אור השי"ת, וזה בתרי בשבא איקבע ירחא. ובאמת אמר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה אשר אלו ואלו דברי אלהים חיים, היינו אם האדם מבקע את ההסתר מכיר אשר כח קדושתו אשר יש בו כח להרחיב את הד"ת, הוא הכל יען אשר יש בו קדושת שבת שקבוע וקיימא, ואז נותן לו השי"ת הד"ת בקביעות ויש לו חלק גם בקדושת שבת שקבוע וקיימא, אשר לזאת הקדושה אין אדם מגיע בפעולותיו, מ"מ יש לו חלק בה ג"כ:
records.targetEnglish: In truth, where does Israel obtain the power to sanctify the festivals and New Moons? It is all because Israel possesses the holiness of Shabbat, which is fixed and enduring, as stated in the holy Zohar, Terumah 135: “We receive the Oral Torah from the Written Torah,” and likewise the holiness of a festival from the holiness of Shabbat. This is the meaning of the opinion that the New Moon was established on the first day of the week: immediately after Shabbat, without any interruption between Shabbat’s holiness and that of the New Moon, so that they would recognize that all their holiness and preparation flow from Shabbat’s holiness. The other opinion says that the New Moon was established on the second day of the week: an ordinary weekday intervened. The light of Shabbat’s holiness was concealed from them, and it appeared that they possessed the power to act; afterward they broke through this concealment and prepared themselves for God’s light. This is the second-day opinion. In truth, my grandfather of blessed memory explained that these and those are the words of the living God. When a person breaks through the concealment, he recognizes that his power of holiness, through which he can extend the Torah’s application, comes entirely from the fixed and enduring holiness of Shabbat. God then grants him an enduring share in the Torah, and he also has a portion in Shabbat’s fixed holiness: although a person cannot reach that holiness through his own acts, he nevertheless has a portion in it too.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains how the two sides can belong to one process. Even the capacity by which Israel sanctifies time is received from Shabbat’s prior holiness; concealment allows that capacity to be experienced as preparation and then recognized as a gift. This deepens Rav Tzadok’s distinction between God’s perspective and Israel’s cherished participation. Neither passage changes the actual precedence of offerings discussed in Zevachim.

records.themeTitle: The desire to fear is already a beginning
records.themeSummary: The difficulty of attaining awe need not prevent a sincere desire for it; the heart’s willingness opens toward a refinement God grants.
records.originHebrew: וְכָתוּב מָה הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹהֶיךָ שׁוֹאֵל כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה וְגוֹמֵר אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא דָּבָר קָשֶׁה מְאֹד לְבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אִם תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְגוֹמֵר אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם וְגוֹמֵר וְכֵן הָיָה טַעֲנַת הַמְרַגְּלִים אֶפֶס כִּי עַז וְגוֹמֵר דִּיהֵא לֵיהּ עוּתְרָא סַגִּי. וְגַם יְלִידֵי הָעֲנָק בָּעֵי גּוּפָא תַּקִּיף גִּיבָּר כַּאֲרִי כּוּלֵּי עֲמָלֵק יוֹשֵׁב וְגוֹמֵר הָא יִצְרָא בִּישָׁא קָטֵיגוֹרָא וְכוּלֵּי וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ. וְעַל זֶה הֵשִׁיבוּ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְכָלֵב דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא לָא בָּעֵי מִנַּן אֶלָּא רְעוּתָא דְּלִבָּא וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בִּתְפִלַּת אַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה (נְחֶמְיָה א׳:י״א) תְּהִי נָא אָזְנְךָ קַשֶּׁבֶת וְגוֹמֵר וְאֶל תְּפִלַּת עֲבָדֶיךָ הַחֲפֵצִים לְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמֶךָ. לֹא אָמַר יִרְאֵי שְׁמֶךָ רַק הַחֲפֵצִים לְיִרְאָה דְּהַיְינוּ רְעוּתָא דְּלִבָּא וְאַחַר כָּךְ חוֹנֵן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ מִצִּדּוֹ לְהִתְבָּרֵר בְּכָל הַמִּדּוֹת.
records.originEnglish: It says, “What does Hashem your God ask, except to fear,” and so forth. Yet in truth, thoroughly refining oneself in the quality of awe is very difficult, as it says, “If you seek it like silver,” and so forth, “then you will understand the fear of Hashem,” and so forth. This was also the spies’ argument: “However, the people are strong,” and so forth—one would need abundant wealth. “And also the descendants of the giant”—one would need a robust body, mighty as a lion … “Amalek dwells,” and so forth—there is the evil inclination, the accuser … as explained in the holy Zohar. Yehoshua and Kalev answered that the Holy One, blessed be He, asks of us only the desire of the heart. This accords with the prayer of the Men of the Great Assembly (Nechemiah 1:11): “Let Your ear be attentive,” and so forth, “and to the prayer of Your servants who desire to fear Your Name.” It does not say “those who fear Your Name,” but “those who desire to fear”—the desire of the heart. Afterward, God graciously grants from His side the ability to become refined in all the qualities.

records.targetEnglish: Fear is different: the one who fears and the one whom he fears are necessarily unlike; they do not share the same quality, for one fears and the other imposes and gives the awe. Therefore, when the attribute of severity above is awakened and thereby gives rise to fear in the human heart—as in the saying, “When the Holy One, blessed be He, executes judgment upon the wicked, He is feared”—this is not called an awakening from above that precedes an awakening from below, since the two are not one and the same thing. Thus, although fear too does not originate with the person, and therefore it says, “Who has preceded Me, that I should repay?”—for here too God acts first by bringing him something that awakens fear—it is nevertheless called an awakening from below. That event does not produce its response with the direct certainty of love giving rise to love, as in “Draw me after You; let us run” and “Bring us back.” Love of this kind applies to Israel, of whom it says, “I have loved you, says Hashem,” because they are called “My twin,” as it were, and such love applies to them. Fear, by contrast, also exists among the nations, though as a very low form of fear, fear of His punishments. The awakening of severity can generate fear, yet its response does not follow with certainty: of the nations it says, “When he is hungry, he will become enraged and curse his king and his God.” The awakening of severity and anger can instead stir a desire to prevail, rage, become angry, and rebel, as it were, against God. Only those described as “desiring to fear Your Name” and searching as for hidden treasures to understand the fear of Hashem will find it. Therefore it is called an awakening from below. This is the whole matter of the Torah, which issues from the side of severity and commands and warns the person to strive to choose the good through his own awakening.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin resolves a difficulty implicit in this paragraph: how can awe be the person’s work if God also awakens it? The divine occasion does not compel the right response; a person can resist it or choose to seek awe. Thus the sincere desire praised here is a real exercise of responsibility, while the power and eventual refinement remain gifts from God.

records.originEnglish: The Chanukah miracle likewise came from God’s side. The commandment of the Temple lamps is, “Come and give Me light” (as stated in Midrash Rabbah, Beha‘alotecha). Yet at the time of the miracle, the light itself came chiefly from God. Only the desire of the heart came from Israel: they wished to kindle the lamps with pure oil. Presumably, when they found a flask containing enough oil for one night, they lit it that night. Afterward, when they would have no pure oil, they would be permitted to use impure oil, because ritual impurity is permitted for communal service (as the Pnei Yehoshua raises in his question in Shabbat). Even if it were not permitted, they would be exempt, for the Torah exempts someone prevented by circumstances beyond his control. Then, on the first day, the miracle had already occurred: by morning the oil had not diminished, and the lamps were full, or the flask was full (as the Beit Yosef explains, Orach Chayim 670). The lamp therefore shone and burned entirely through God’s action.
records.targetHebrew: וכל זה הוא כשאדם הולך מצידו בעבודה וצמצום. אבל אם אדם אין לו שום צמצום מצידו, ורק מתפשט עצמו בכל מיני התפשטות, ואינו רוצה בתפיסתו שום עבודה וצמצום, והגם שאחר כך רואה שאי אפשר לעשות שום פעולה בלתי רצון השי"ת, מ"מ מאחר שמצידו לא רצה להכיר זאת ממילא הוא ותפיסתו יאבד לגמרי. אבל מי שהולך מצידו בצמצום ועבודה, ורק שנסתר לפעמים ממנו אור ד' זה היה עבודתו של כהן להעלות זאת הפעולה ג"כ להשי"ת, וגמר זה הבירור אי אפשר להיות ע"י בשר ודם ורק מהשי"ת בעצמו. וזה שכתיב אל מול פני המנורה יאירו שבעת הנרות, היינו שגמר ההדלקה תהיה מאליה היינו מצד השי"ת, והיינו שיעבוד לפי כחו והגמר יברר השי"ת, ובעשיה כתיב העלה נרותיה היינו מאחר שבירר עצמו לפי כחו, אז אומר השי"ת שאפילו זה הגמר נקרא על שם האדם, וזה שלא שינה:
records.targetEnglish: All this the retrospective clarification through repentance applies when a person proceeds, from his own side, through service and restraint. But if he practices no restraint and simply spreads out in every direction, unwilling to accept any service or restraint within his own awareness, then although afterward he sees that no act is possible without God’s will, nevertheless, since from his own side he did not wish to recognize this, he and his own grasp are lost entirely. By contrast, when a person proceeds through restraint and service, but God’s light is sometimes concealed from him, the priest’s work is to raise even such an act to God. The completion of this clarification cannot come through flesh and blood, but only from God Himself. This is the meaning of “Toward the face of the menorah the seven lamps shall shine”: the completion of the lighting is to occur of itself, from God. The person must work according to his strength, and God will clarify the completion. Yet in the account of the act it says, “He raised its lamps”: once he has clarified himself according to his strength, God says that even this completion is called by the person’s name. This is “he did not change.”
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the menorah’s wording as a precise relation between human effort and divine completion: the person works as far as he can, and God completes what no person can finish. This illuminates why the oil miracle does not make Israel’s willing action superfluous. Its explicit requirement of service and restraint also prevents recognition of divine action from becoming a claim that personal responsibility is unnecessary.

records.targetEnglish: Through this sanctification of God’s name they merited the miracle of the oil, by which God showed them that they were worthy to give light before Him in the Temple, from which light goes forth to the world. This is the meaning of the commandment of the Temple lamps: to give light before Him in the dark passageways, for this world is darkened from God’s light through the nations. As the Midrash says of Abraham our father, he came and gave light before Him, as it were, in the dark passageways—that is, by making His divinity known to the nations. This was also the purpose of all the Temple service, where the Divine Presence was revealed in order to make His divinity known. Lighting the lamps gives light to everyone who comes into the world, including those in the deepest darkness. Therefore the wording of Al HaNissim specifies, out of all the acts of service, that they lit lamps: this was the essential completion of the attribute of Hod that they repaired then. The miracle that occurred for them in this act is not mentioned, because it is not the matter of the miracle and deliverance of Chanukah itself. Rather, it was what Heaven revealed to them: that they had found favor before Him and had completed the repair, to the point that Heaven assisted them in giving light before Him.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains what the divine assistance disclosed: acceptance of Israel’s service and restoration of the capacity to make God’s presence known. In its complete context, this acceptance follows Israel’s self-sacrifice to sanctify God’s name. This adds the purpose of the gifted light to Pri Tzadik’s account of its source. The quoted distinction between military deliverance and the oil’s disclosure of favor is retained, rather than treating every mention of a miracle as interchangeable.

records.targetHebrew: עַל יְדֵי הַחֵשֶׁק הוּא כְּלִי קִבּוּל לְהַשְׁרָאַת שְׁכִינַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹ. וְזֶהוּ תְּרוּמַת הַמִּשְׁכָּן: "מֵאֵת כָּל אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִדְּבֶנּוּ לִבּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ב), דִּנְדִיבוּת הַלֵּב דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא בִּנְיַן הַמִּשְׁכָּן דִּשְׁכִינַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים. וּבָזֶה הוּא כָּל חַד לְפוּם מַה דִּמְשַׁעֵר בְּלִבֵּיהּ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה הַרְגָּשַׁת אֶחָד מִשְׁכַּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּלִבּוֹ לַחֲבֵירוֹ; כִּי כְּפִי נְדִיבַת לְבָבוֹ בְּתִגְבּוֹרֶת חֶשְׁקוֹ לְהַשִּׂיג, כָּךְ הוּא שְׁכִינַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.  וְיֵשׁ עוֹד תְּרוּמַת הָאֲדָנִים וּדְקָרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהּ: "הֶעָשִׁיר לֹא יַרְבֶּה וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת ל, טו), שֶׁבֵּין הֶעָשִׁיר בְּדַעַת וּבְהַרְגָּשַׁת הַלֵּב וְתִגְבּוֹרֶת הַחֵשֶׁק, וּבֵין הֶעָנִי – שָׁוִים בַּחֲלָקִים; כִּי הוּא "לְכַפֵּר עַל נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם" כִּמְפוֹרָשׁ בַּכָּתוּב, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי דִּשְׁקָלִים (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ד): דִּלְכַפֵּר אַעֵגֶל; פֵּירוּשׁ: לְקַנֵּחַ לִכְלוּךְ דְּחֶשְׁקוֹת רָעוֹת מִן הַלֵּב. וְכֵן בְּקָרְבְּנוֹת צִבּוּר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה פִּינְחָס): "תָּמִיד שֶׁל שַׁחַר מְכַפֵּר וְכוּלֵי"; וּבְעִנְיַן הַרְחָקָה מִן הָרַע כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁוִים, שֶׁכֻּלָּם יוּכְלוּ לִינָּקוֹת מִן הָרַע בְּתַכְלִית, רַק חִלּוּק הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת הוּא בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַטּוֹב.
records.targetEnglish: Through yearning a person becomes a vessel for the indwelling of God’s presence within his heart. This is the contribution for the Mishkan, “From every person whose heart moves him”: through the generosity of Israel’s hearts the Mishkan is built, the dwelling of God in the lower realm. In this matter, each person experiences it according to the measure of his heart. One person’s sense of God dwelling within him is unlike another’s, for the indwelling corresponds to the generosity of his heart and the strength of his yearning to attain it. There is also the contribution for the sockets and for the offerings, concerning which it says, “The rich shall not give more.” The one rich in understanding, feeling of the heart, and strength of yearning, and the poor person, contribute equal portions, because it is “to atone for your lives,” as Scripture states. The Jerusalem Talmud, Shekalim, explains that it atones for the calf: that is, to cleanse the heart of the stain of evil desires. Likewise, concerning the communal offerings the Sages said that the morning daily offering atones. In distancing themselves from evil all Israel are equal, for all can become completely clean of evil; differences of degree concern the attainment of the good.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the inward construction that Pri Tzadik names: a person’s yearning becomes a vessel for God’s dwelling. It also distinguishes different intensities of inward reception from the shared capacity and obligation to turn from evil. Thus “every heart” does not require identical spiritual attainment, and the sanctuary remains grounded in actual work on the heart.

records.targetHebrew: אלא ישראל מצדם יש להם מבינות בעומק לבם אשר אין להם מצדם שום שלימות בלתי עבודה לכך הם משתוקקים תמיד לעבודת השי"ת ולפיכך חפץ בהם השי"ת ג"כ וזהו כענין שמצינו בגמ' (מגילה כו) והי' בנימין הצדיק מצטער עלי' לבולעה שנאמר חופף עליו כל היום לפיכך זכה בנימין ונעשה אושפיזכן לשכינה וכו' היינו משום שהי' משתוקק תמיד לאור לפיכך זכה ונעשה אושפיזכן לשכינה ככה משום שידע השי"ת אם יפתח לישראל מעט אור יהיו משתוקקים ביותר שיפתח להם השי"ת יותר אור לפיכך שוכן בהם השי"ת וחפץ בעבודתם וזהו כדאיתא בזוה"ק (תרומה קכח) ומנא ידעינן דקוב"ה איתרעי בי' ושוי' מדורי' בי' כד חמינון דרעותא דההוא בר נש בחדוה ברעותא דלבא למרדף ולאשתדלא אבתרי' דקב"ה בלבי' ובנפשי' וברעותא ודאי תמן ידעינן דשרי' בי' שכינתא וכו' היינו מזה שרואים שישראל מבקשים ומשתוקקים כ"כ לעבודה ממילא נתברר מזה דאתרעי בהו קוב"ה ושי' מדורי' בהו וממילא נתברר מזה ג"כ שרק ישראל המה נקיים אגב אמם ועלה במחשבה אבל לא עמלק ולכך צריכין ישראל תמיד לעבודה ולבל יבטחו את עצמם על זאת התקיפות שעתיד השי"ת לברר את ישראל משום שהמה נקיים אגב אמם כי נגד זאת התקיפות נתעורר תמיד הקיטרוג של עמלק שאומר שהוא ג"כ נקי אגב אמו ולזה כאשר יניח משה ידו וגבר וגו':
records.targetEnglish: Israel, from their own side, understand in the depth of the heart that they have no completeness without service. They therefore constantly yearn for the service of God, and God likewise desires them. This resembles what we find in the Gemara: Binyamin the righteous longed to absorb the altar’s strip of land into his portion, as it says, “He hovers over it all day”; therefore Binyamin merited becoming the host of the Divine Presence. Because he constantly yearned for the light, he merited becoming its host. In the same way, because God knew that if He opened a little light for Israel they would yearn still more for Him to open greater light, He dwells among them and desires their service. As the holy Zohar says: “How do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, desires him and has placed His dwelling within him? When we see that the will of this person is joyfully, with the heart’s desire, to pursue and strive after the Holy One, blessed be He, with heart, soul, and will—then we certainly know that the Divine Presence dwells within him.” That is, from seeing how much Israel seeks and yearns for service, it becomes clear that the Holy One desires them and has made His dwelling among them. This also reveals that Israel alone is pure by virtue of its source and arose in the divine thought, unlike Amalek. Therefore Israel always needs service and must not rely upon the assurance that God will ultimately clarify Israel because of its purity at the source. Against that assurance Amalek’s accusation is always aroused, claiming that it too is pure by virtue of its source. Therefore, “When Moshe lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives a test and a continuing condition for the inward dwelling: the heart keeps seeking a fuller relation to God through service. Binyamin’s yearning supplies its concrete sanctuary model. The passage’s final warning preserves the distinction between recognizing an enduring divine bond and treating that bond as a reason to dispense with work.

records.originHebrew: וְהַמְכוּוָּן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר כְּבִרְכָתוֹ בֵּרַךְ אוֹתָם לְפִי שֶׁבֵּירְכָן יְהוּדָה בְּאַרְיֵה וְכוּלֵּי חָזַר וּכְלָלָן כּוּלָּן כְּא׳ וַעֲשָׂאָן אֲרָיוֹת וְכוּלֵּי וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל קְדוּשּׁוֹת הַשְּׁבָטִים כְּלוּלִים זֶה בָּזֶה. וְכָל א׳ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כָּלוּל מִקְּדוּשַּׁת כָּל הַי״ב שְׁבָטִים. וְאַף שֶׁקְּדוּשַּׁת יוֹסֵף מוֹרֶה שֶׁהָעִיקָּר עֲבוֹדַת הָאָדָם לְהִתְבָּרֵר בְּמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁמִּטַּעַם זֶה הִקְדִּים מְנַשֶּׁה לְאֶפְרַיִם. מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּלוּל בּוֹ גַּם קְדוּשַּׁת כָּל הַשְּׁבָטִים וּבְתוֹכָם שֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָה שֶׁקְּדוּשָּׁתוֹ בְּחִינַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁאָמַר הַשֵּׁם רוֹעִי וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁמּוֹרֶה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרֵךְ וְאֵין לְהָאָדָם מֵהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ כְּלוּם.
records.originEnglish: The meaning follows Bereishit Rabbah on the verse, “Each according to his blessing, he blessed them”: “Since he blessed Yehudah as a lion … he then included them all together and made them all lions …” All the tribes’ distinctive forms of holiness are included within one another. Every Jew contains the holiness of all twelve tribes. Yosef’s holiness indicates that a person’s chief service is to refine himself in awe—the aspect represented by Yosef. As we explained, this is why he placed Menashe before Ephraim. Nevertheless, he also contains the holiness of all the tribes, including Yehudah, whose holiness is represented by King David, peace be upon him, who said, “Hashem is my shepherd,” and so forth, indicating that everything comes from God, and a person possesses nothing independently through his own effort.
records.targetHebrew: דְּכָל שֵׁבֶט יֵשׁ לוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא מְיוּחָד וּמְנוּשָּׂא עַל כָּל הַשְּׁבָטִים וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכּוּלָּם ״גּוֹי אֶחָד״ (שְׁמוּאֵל ב ז:כג), וּקְדֻשַּׁת כָּל אֶחָד כָּלוּל בְּכוּלָּם מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּדָבָר זֶה הוּא הָרֹאשׁ, וְכֹחוֹ הוּא שֶׁמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בְּכוּלָּם וְהַכֹּל מֵעֲנָפָיו
records.targetEnglish: For every tribe has something in which it is distinctive and elevated above all the other tribes. Although they are all one nation, and each one’s holiness is included in them all, nevertheless, in this particular matter that tribe is the head: its power extends into them all, and all are branches of it.
records.explanation: This concise distinction explains how the whole can be present in each person while one quality remains a tribe’s leading strength. Yosef can lead in disciplined awe without excluding Yehudah’s recognition of dependence on God; the strength of each is received by the others from its particular root.

records.targetHebrew: דְּהִנֵּה בְּהַשְּׁנֵים עָשָׂר שִׁבְטֵי יָ"הּ נָתַן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אוֹר וְחַיִּים שֶׁאֵין אֶחָד דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵרוֹ, וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָאִים גְּבוּלֵי אֲלַכְסוֹן הַיְינוּ שֶׁאוֹרוֹ שֶׁל זֶה הוּא הֵיפֶךְ מִשֶּׁל זֶה, כִּי לָזֶה נִמְשָׁךְ כֹּחַ חִיּוּתוֹ מִמִּדַּת הָאַהֲבָה וְלָזֶה מִמִּדַּת הַיִּרְאָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה. וַעֲבוּר זֶה נִמְצָא כָּל הַפְּלוּגְתּוֹת בַּגְּמָרָא אַף כִּי הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם אֶחָד כְּדֵי לְקַיֵּים רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצָאנוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (פְּסָחִים נּוּן גִּימֶל עַמּוּד בֵּית) "בֵּין שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְהַדְלִיק וּבֵין שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַדְלִיק שְׁנֵיהֶם לְדָבָר אֶחָד נִתְכַּוְּונוּ", וְכֵן הוּא כָּל הַפְּלוּגְתּוֹת כִּי מְקוֹרָם מִמָּקוֹם אֶחָד וְלָכֵן נִקְרָאִים שְׁבָטִים מִלְּשׁוֹן עֲנָפִים שֶׁמִּתְפַּשְּׁטִים לְכָאן וּלְכָאן. וְהוּא שֶׁהִנִּיחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשֵׁבֶט גָּד מִדַּת יִסּוּרִין כִּי זֶה הַשֵּׁבֶט אוֹמֵר כִּי בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה בְּלֵב הָאָדָם בְּלֹא יִסּוּרִין, וּבְדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם מִי שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל יִסּוּרִין אֵין לוֹ כָּל כָּךְ שִׂמְחָה וְאֵינוֹ כָּל כָּךְ בְּצַוְותָּא עִם בְּנֵי אָדָם. וְלָכֵן נִתְבָּרְכוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם שִׂמְחָה וְצַוְותָּא, וּבֵרֵךְ אוֹתָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם הִתְחַבְּרוּת וְיִהְיֶה בָּהֶם גְּדוּדִים גְּדוּדִים, וְלָכֵן לֹא נִמְצָא בְּשׁוּם שֵׁבֶט שֶׁיִּכְלוֹל כָּל הַמִּסְפָּרִים הַיְינוּ מֵאוֹת וַאֲלָפִים וַעֲשָׂרוֹת רַק בְּשֵׁבֶט גָּד מַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ בִּשְׁאָר הַשְּׁבָטִים, "וְהוּא יָגֻד עָקֵב" הַיְינוּ בִּזְמַן שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ לְקַבֵּץ אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אָז הוּא יֶאֱגוֹד וְיִקְשׁוֹר אֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּמִמֶּנּוּ יָבֹא כָּל מִינֵי שִׂמְחָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי אֵלִיָּהוּ הוּא מִשֵּׁבֶט גָּד כַּנִּזְכָּר בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עַיִן אָלֶף, יוֹד בֵּית).
records.targetEnglish: Within the twelve tribes of God, the Holy One, blessed be He, placed light and life unlike that of any other tribe. They are therefore called diagonal boundaries: the light of one is the opposite of another’s, for one draws the force of its life from love, another from awe, and so forth. From this come all the disputes in the Gemara, although everything goes to one place, to fulfill God’s will. As we find in Pesachim 53b: whether they said to kindle or not to kindle, both intended the same thing. So it is with all the disputes, for their source is one place. They are therefore called shevatim, branches spreading in different directions. God placed in the tribe of Gad the quality of suffering, for this tribe says that Torah cannot enter the human heart without suffering. Ordinarily, a person who suffers lacks a measure of joy and companionship. They were therefore blessed with joy and companionship; he blessed them with connection, so that they would form bands together. Thus no other tribe’s count includes all the orders—hundreds, thousands, and tens—as Gad’s does. “He will gather at the end” means that when Israel needs to be assembled, he will bind and join all Israel, and from him every kind of joy will come to Israel, for Eliyahu is from the tribe of Gad, as stated in the Midrash.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach makes the complementary structure concrete: the tribe whose particular approach emphasizes suffering is blessed to become a source of companionship and joy. This shows what it means for an opposite quality to complete rather than cancel a tribe’s leading character. The need for suffering is explicitly Gad’s particular perspective in this account, not a universal prerequisite newly imposed on every reader.

records.originHebrew: וְאִיתָא (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה מ) אֵין לְךָ גָּדוֹל מִשֵּׁבֶט יְהוּדָה וְאֵין לְךָ יָרוּד מִשֵּׁבֶט דָּן כּוּלֵּי אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יָבֹא וְיִזְדַּוֵּוג לוֹ כּוּלֵּי הַמִּשְׁכָּן בִּשְׁנֵי שְׁבָטִים אֵלּוּ נַעֲשָׂה וְכֵן הַמִּקְדָּשׁ כּוּלֵּי עַיֵּין שָׁם וּבַזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג קצד ב) אִיתָא שֶׁגַּם לֶעָתִיד יָבֹא שְׂרָיָה מִשֵּׁבֶט דָּן עִם מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף. וְיִהְיֶה שֵׁבֶט דָּן מְשׁוּתָּף גַּם בְּבִנְיַן הֶעָתִיד. וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּסָבָא (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דָּן וְנַפְתָּלִי גָּד וְאָשֵׁר בְּיַרְכָא שְׂמָאלָא דָּן עַד פִּרְקָא דְּרַגְלָא כּוּלֵּי וְהַיְינוּ כְּנֶגֶד מִדַּת הוֹד. וְעַל כֵּן הוּא מְשׁוּתָּף לְבִנְיַן הַמִּשְׁכָּן וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
records.originEnglish: Shemot Rabbah (end of section 40) states, “No tribe is greater than Yehudah, and none is lowlier than Dan … The Holy One, blessed be He, said, ‘Let the latter come and join him’ … The Mishkan was made through these two tribes, and likewise the Temple …” See there. The holy Zohar (III, 194b) states that in the future Seraiah from the tribe of Dan will come with Mashiach ben Yosef. The tribe of Dan will thus also participate in the future building. This follows the teaching in Sava (Zohar II, 104, end of side b): “Dan, Naftali, Gad, and Asher correspond to the left leg; Dan extends as far as the joint of the leg …” This corresponds to the attribute of Hod. Dan therefore shares in the construction of the Mishkan and the Temple.
records.targetHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא ״אַרְיֵה״ כִּיהוּדָה, וּבְכָל מָקוֹם מְחוּבָּר לִיהוּדָה כַּנּוֹדָע בִּמְלֶאכֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְהַמִּקְדָּשׁ [בְּצַלְאֵל מִיהוּדָה וְאָהֳלִיאָב מִדָּן], וְגַם לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר וְהוּא מִצַּד מִדַּת הָעִגּוּלִים דְּהָרֹאשׁ וְהַסּוֹף מְחוּבָּר יַחַד וְגַם ״זַנְבָא דְּאַרְיֵה הוּא, וְדָן יָדִין עַמּוֹ כְּאֶחָד״ וְגוֹמֵר — מְיוּחָד שֶׁבַּשְּׁבָטִים, זֶה יְהוּדָה
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, Dan is called a lion like Yehudah, and everywhere he is joined to Yehudah, as is known concerning the work of the Mishkan and the Temple—Betzalel from Yehudah and Oholiav from Dan—and also in the days of Mashiach, as stated in the Zohar. This is from the aspect of the circles, in which the beginning and the end are joined together. He is also “the lion’s tail,” and “Dan shall judge his people as one”—like the most distinguished of the tribes, Yehudah.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin gives a structural reason for the partnership: at the level figured as a circle, the first and last meet. Dan’s low position in an ordered body therefore does not place him outside its unity. The preceding discussion proposes a different month arrangement and expressly acknowledges multiple arrangements; this comparison uses its explanation of Dan and Yehudah’s partnership, without equating that calendar with Pri Tzadik’s Tevet correspondence.

records.targetHebrew:
אלה פקודי המשכן משכן העדות אשר פקד על פי משה וגו'.
ביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה בספרו הקדוש (מי השלוח ח"א פקודי ד"ה אלה) שעדות נקרא דבר מבורר ומפורש, כדאיתא בש"ס (ר"ה כ"ד.) ראינוהו בעששית אין מעידין עליו וכו' ראינוהו מאלינו ושבנו לראותו מדעתינו ולא ראינוהו אין מעידין עליו, כי עדות נקרא רק דבר מפורש. וזה משכן העדות, וכדאיתא בש"ס (שבת כ"ב:) עדות הוא לכל באי עולם שהשכינה שורה בישראל, היינו שבגמר בנין המשכן הכיר כל אחד ואחד דבר מבורר ומפורש, איך שהשי"ת שוכן אצל כל אחד ואחד מישראל. והוא, כי באמת הנדיבות לבנין המשכן לא היה כל אחד ואחד בשוה, יש אשר היה לו יותר נדיבות ויש אשר לא היה לו כ"כ נדיבות. וכל אחד ואחד הביא כפי התנדבותו, ובגמר המשכן כשהיה צריך להקימו, הכירו כל אחד ואחד מפורש, אשר כמו שלא היה יכול להקים את המשכן בלא אדם זה אשר יש לו נדיבות גדולה, כן לא היה יכול להקימו גם בלא זה אשר לא היה לו נדיבות כ"כ, וממילא הכירו כולם עדות מבוררת ומפורשת אשר הנדיבות שלהם מן גדלם ועד קטנם המה מבוררים, והשי"ת שוכן בכל אחד ואחד מישראל:
records.targetEnglish: “These are the accounts of the Mishkan, the Mishkan of testimony, which were counted at Moshe’s command,” and so forth. My grandfather explained in his holy book Mei HaShiloach that testimony means something clarified and explicit. As the Gemara says, seeing the New Moon in a glass lantern is insufficient for testimony; likewise, if they saw it incidentally, returned to look deliberately, and did not see it, they cannot testify. Testimony means something explicit. This is the “Mishkan of testimony,” as the Gemara says: “It is testimony to everyone who comes into the world that the Divine Presence dwells among Israel.” At the completion of the Mishkan, each person recognized clearly and explicitly how God dwells with every Jew. The generosity shown in building the Mishkan was not equal: one person had greater generosity, another less, and each brought according to his willingness. When the completed Mishkan needed to be erected, everyone recognized explicitly that just as it could not be erected without the person of great generosity, neither could it be erected without the person whose generosity was less. They all therefore recognized with clear and explicit testimony that the generosity of all, from the greatest to the least, was accepted as genuine, and that God dwells in each and every Jew.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why including the less prominent participant is essential to a divine dwelling. The completed sanctuary itself reveals that the greater contribution could not substitute for the smaller one. This illuminates Pri Tzadik’s insistence on Dan’s actual partnership, rather than reducing his inclusion to a general expression of goodwill.

records.themeSummary: Moshe and Aharon, figured as the two legs, restore the connection to Yaakov’s unified body; Chanukah likewise builds a dwelling for the Divine Presence.
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא דְּיָדוּעַ דְּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן תְּרֵין יַרְכִין נֵצַח וְהוֹד. וְהֵם קֵירְבוּ הַכֹּל לִבְחִינַת יַעֲקֹב גּוּפָא לְתַקֵּן מַה דִּכְתִיב וַתֵּקַע כַּף יֶרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב וְאִיתָא (חוּלִּין צא.) וְרַבָּנַן מֵאֲחוֹרֵיהּ אֲתָא וְנַשְּׁיֵיהּ בְּתַרְוַיְיהוּ. וּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן יְתַקְּנוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם. וְכֵן מִצְוַת נֵרוֹת חֲנוּכָּה עַד יוֹם ח׳ שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הוֹד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתִיקּוּנֵי הַזּוֹהַר (שָׁם) וְאִיהוּ הוֹד תְּמָנְיָא יוֹמֵי דַּחֲנוּכָּה שֶׁעִנְיַן חֲנוּכָּה הוּא גַּם כֵּן לַעֲשׂוֹת מִקְדָּשׁ וּבַיִת לְהַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה וְעַל זֶה עוֹשִׂין חֲנוּכַּת הַבַּיִת:
records.originEnglish: For Moshe and Aharon are known to represent the two legs, Netzach and Hod. They brought everyone near to the aspect of Yaakov, represented by the torso, to repair what is described by “The socket of Yaakov’s thigh was dislocated.” The Gemara (Chullin 91a) states that the Rabbis hold that the angel “came from behind him and struck him in both thighs.” Moshe and Aharon will repair both. Likewise, the commandment of the Chanukah lights extends through the eighth day, which represents Hod, as Tikkunei Zohar says there, “It is Hod, the eight days of Chanukah.” For Chanukah too is about making a sanctuary and a dwelling for the Shekhinah, and for this we hold the dedication of the dwelling.
records.targetHebrew: היינו כי אחר שעובד האדם באלו המדות אז מכיר בשורש אחדותן דלית שם מכל אינון מדות כלל ועל הנס של חנוכה ופורים איתא בהאר"י הק' ז"ל שהי' בנצח והוד שנראה לתרי פלגא דגופא כדאיתא בזוה"ק (פנחס רלו.) ונקראו בתקוני זוה"ק (תיקן יג לא:) תרין ירכין וכו' שהם לבר מגופא (זוה"ק בראשית כא:) היינו אחר שיוצא על הפעולה ובכל זאת ניכר גם שם האחדות כשהולך דרך יעקב אבינו שהוא מכיר איך שהשי"ת הוא מנושא ומשולל מכל המדות
records.targetEnglish: After a person serves through these attributes kindness and severity, Netzach and Hod, he recognizes the unity at their root, where none of these differentiated attributes applies. Concerning the miracles of Chanukah and Purim, the holy Ari teaches that they were in Netzach and Hod, which appear as two halves of a body. They are called “the two thighs” in Tikkunei Zohar, “outside the body” in the Zohar—that is, after the inner powers emerge into action. Even there the unity is recognizable when one follows the path of Yaakov our father, who recognizes how God is exalted beyond and free of all the attributes.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the significance of the bodily image itself: the legs represent the movement from inner qualities into actual deeds, where separation can appear most pronounced. Yaakov’s path reveals the unity there too. This gives conceptual force to Pri Tzadik’s account of repairing both legs and making an earthly dwelling through Chanukah’s acts.

records.themeTitle: Disagreement that seeks a connecting understanding
records.themeSummary: The Torah’s “wars” can begin in opposition and end in love through the work of learning together.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ הַדְּרָשׁ נִדְרָשׁ עַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְזֶהוּ מִלְחֲמוֹת הַשֵּׁם שֶׁעַל יְדֵי סֵפֶר וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִידּוּשִׁין ל:) אֲפִילּוּ אָב וּבְנוֹ הָרַב וְתַלְמִידוֹ שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה בְּשַׁעַר א׳ נַעֲשִׂים אוֹיְבִים זֶה אֶת זֶה וְאֵינָם זָזִים מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשִׂין אוֹהֲבִין זֶה אֶת זֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אֶת וָהֵב בְּסוּפָה כּוּלֵּי וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמְרוּ שִׁירָה עַל הַבְּאֵר שֶׁהוּא מְרַמֵּז לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
records.originEnglish: Homiletically, the passage is expounded as referring to the Oral Torah. These are “the wars of Hashem” conducted through a book of Torah. As the Sages said (Kiddushin 30b), even a father and son, or a teacher and student, studying Torah at one gate become enemies of one another, yet they do not leave until they love one another, as it says, “Et Vahev in Suphah,” and so forth. Afterward they sang concerning the well, which alludes to the Oral Torah.
records.targetHebrew: וּשְׁנֵי הָאֲחֵרִים הֵם כְּשֶׁמְּחַדְּשִׁין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְאָז נִקְרָא "יִרְאֵי ה'", וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת דְּנֹעַם וְחוֹבְלִים הַנִּדְרָשׁ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.) עַל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבָבֶל. וְהַנּוֹחִין זֶה נֹעַם, וְאֵלּוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם נִקְרְאוּ יִרְאֵי ה' שֶׁאֵינָם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַקְשִׁיב – פֵּירוּשׁ מְקַבֵּל מַה שֶּׁהֵם גּוֹזְרִים, דְּזֶה נִקְרָא "אֲחוֹתִי", שֶׁחִדּוּשִׁים שֶׁלָּהֶם מְקוּבָּלִים וּמוּסְכָּמִים לְמַעְלָה, וּבִתְנַאי שֶׁיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם יִרְאֵי ה'. וְעִיקַּר הַרְבָּצַת תּוֹרָה הָיְתָה בְּבָבֶל כִּדְאִיתָא בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (קו.), כִּי רִבּוּי הַתַּלְמִידִים הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַפִּלְפּוּל וְהַחִידּוּד שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת וְהַהֲפָכִין, וְזֶהוּ הַמְּחַדְּדִין, עַל יְדֵי זֶה עוֹלִין לִגְדוּלָּה דְּהַיְינוּ הַעֲמָדַת תַּלְמִידִים. כִּי שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים עַל כָּרְחֲךָ צְרִיכִין לְאֶמְצָעִי וְדַעַת הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "וַהֲדָרְךָ",
records.targetEnglish: The other two levels of companionship occur when they develop new Torah teachings; then they are called “those who fear Hashem.” These are the two levels of “Pleasantness” and “Wounders,” expounded in Sanhedrin 24 concerning the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel and Babylonia. Those who are gentle with one another correspond to “Pleasantness.” These two gentle study partners are called “those who fear Hashem”; they are not two opposing sides. “The Holy One, blessed be He, listens attentively” means that He accepts what they decree. This is called “My sister”: their new teachings are accepted and agreed to above, on condition that both of them fear Hashem. The chief dissemination of Torah took place in Babylonia, as stated in Ketubot 106, because the increase of students comes through incisive reasoning and sharpening, which develop through disagreement and opposing positions. This is why those who sharpen one another rise to greatness—that is, they establish students. Two opposites necessarily require a mediating element and an understanding that joins them. This is called “your majesty.”
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes gentle partners who share awe from the sharper Babylonian inquiry. In the latter, opposing positions create a need for an understanding that joins the two sides. This explains how the “wars” described here can serve a common Torah inquiry and end in love. The complete target also warns that sharpness can feed pride and expressly requires על דבר אמת וענוה צדק—“for truth, humility, and righteousness”—so the benefit is not attributed to contention by itself.

records.themeTitle: The gift of questions that reach the source
records.themeSummary: Moshe’s generous transmission includes the power of Torah reasoning through which the sages develop new teachings.
records.originHebrew: וְכָתוּב כָּרוּהָ נְדִיבֵי עָם הַיְינוּ מַה שֶׁחִידְּשׁוּ הַחֲכָמִים כָּל א׳ מִלִּבּוֹ וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים. וְנִדְרָשׁ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה שֶׁכָּל א׳ מֵהַנְּשִׂיאִים עוֹמְדִים עַל גַּבָּיו וּמוֹשְׁכִים בְּמַטּוֹתֵיהֶן כָּל א׳ לְשִׁבְטוֹ כּוּלֵּי וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בָּא עַל יְדֵי הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁהֵם נְדִיבֵי עָם. וְכָתוּב בִּמְחֹקֵק שֶׁהָיָה הָעִיקָר עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ שֶׁנִּקְרָא מְחוֹקֵק כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי שָׁם חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק סָפוּן. וְהוּא הוֹרִיד הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב וְהָיָה כָּלוּל בָּהּ כָּל הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְנָהַג בָּהּ טוֹבַת עַיִן וּנְתָנָהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים לח.) וְהַיְינוּ פִילְפּוּלָא בְּעָלְמָא שֶׁנִּיתָּן רַק לְמֹשֶׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם
records.originEnglish: It is also written, “The nobles of the people excavated it.” These are the new teachings that the sages each brought forth from their own hearts; they are the words of the living God. Midrash Rabbah expounds that each of the princes stood over the well and drew its water with his staff, each for his own tribe, and so forth. The Oral Torah comes through the Sanhedrin and the Torah scholars, who are the nobles of the people. The verse continues, “with the lawgiver”: its principal source was Moshe our teacher, who is called the lawgiver, as it says, “For there the lawgiver’s portion is concealed.” He brought down the Written Torah, which contained the entire Oral Torah, and generously gave it to Israel, as the Sages state (Nedarim 38a). This refers specifically to the art of incisive Torah reasoning, which had been given to Moshe alone, as explained there.
records.targetHebrew: ועל זה הענין אמרו ז"ל בגמרא (נדרים לח) שמסר משה בטובת עינו לישראל פלפולי דאורייתא ופלפולי דאורייתא הוא כענין שמצינו בגמרא (ב"מ פד) גבי ר' יוחנן בר לקושא רמי לי כ"ד קושיות וכ"ד פרוקי וממילא רווחא שמעתתא היינו שע"י הפלפול מקושיות ופרוקים נתבררו כל המסכים המסתירים עד שהגיע לעומק השמעתתא וכן הוא הפלפול בכל עניני עוה"ז שישראל אינם בנייחא משום לבוש נמוך מהטובה עד שמגיעין ע"י כמה ברורין לעומק השורש מהטובה וזהו מה דסיים יעקב פתח משה שהראה מ"ר שישראל אינם מתחילין לקבל שום טובה בלעדי עומק הרצון יתברך הנמצא בה:
records.targetEnglish: Concerning this the Sages said in the Gemara, Nedarim 38, that Moshe, in his generosity, transmitted the incisive reasoning of Torah to Israel. Such reasoning is like what we find in Bava Metzia 84 concerning Rabbi Yochanan: “Bar Lakisha would raise twenty-four objections to me, and I would give twenty-four resolutions; thus the teaching became more expansive.” Through the reasoning of questions and resolutions, all the screens that conceal were clarified until he reached the depth of the teaching. The same kind of inquiry applies to all matters of this world: Israel does not find rest in a lowly outer garment of a benefit, but through many clarifications reaches the depth of its source. This is the meaning of “Where Yaakov ended, Moshe began”: Moshe our teacher showed that Israel does not begin to receive any benefit apart from the depth of God’s will found within it.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains what Moshe’s gift of Torah reasoning enables. Questions and answers remove layers of concealment until the learner reaches the source within the teaching. This gives a mechanism to Pri Tzadik’s movement from the Written Torah received by Moshe to new teachings emerging through the sages’ hearts. The target’s extension to other benefits also fits the section’s governing demand to recognize God’s will within what a person receives.

records.themeTitle: Recovering the light concealed in Torah
records.themeSummary: The Torah and the book of Yehoshua already contain what later study must disclose, including the roots of each person’s portion.
records.originHebrew: וּכְבָר אָמַרְנוּ שֶׁזֶּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים כב:) אִלְמָלֵא חָטְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא נִיתָּן לָהֶם אֶלָּא ה׳ חוּמְשֵׁי תּוֹרָה וְסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּלְבַד שֶׁעֶרְכָּהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא. שֶׁהַמְכוּוָּן שֶׁסֵּפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הוּא סוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ מֹשֶׁה קִיבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ דְּקָאֵי עַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב קלז ב) דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב מָסַר לְלֵוָאֵי וְאִלְמָלֵא חָטְאוּ הָיוּ רוֹאִים אֵיךְ הַכֹּל כָּלוּל בְּה׳ חוּמְשֵׁי תּוֹרָה דְּלֵיכָּא מִידֵּי דְּלָא רְמִיזֵי בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ תַּעֲנִית ט.) וְזֶהוּ עֶרְכָּהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהִיא מְקוֹם הַשְּׁכִינָה. וְעֶרְכָּהּ הַיְינוּ חֵלֶק כָּל א׳ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא אֶרֶץ בְּחִינַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל. וְאַף דְּסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ רַק שְׁמוֹת עֲיָירוֹת צְפוּנִים בּוֹ הַסּוֹדוֹת מִשָּׁרְשֵׁי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא סֵפֶר רִאשׁוֹן אַחַר תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה.
records.originEnglish: We have explained that this is the meaning of the saying (Nedarim 22b): had Israel not sinned, they would have been given only the Five Books of the Torah and the book of Yehoshua, which sets out the arrangement of the Land of Israel. The intended meaning is that the book of Yehoshua embodies the mystery of the Oral Torah. Concerning this they said, “Moshe received Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Yehoshua,” referring to the Oral Torah, as the holy Zohar states (II, 137b), for the Written Torah he entrusted to the Levites. Had they not sinned, they would have seen how everything is contained in the Five Books of the Torah, for nothing is without a hint in the Torah (as stated in Ta‘anit 9a). This is the inner arrangement of the Land of Israel, the dwelling place of the Divine Presence. Its arrangement means each Israelite’s portion in the Oral Torah, which is the Land in its aspect as the Congregation of Israel. Although these passages of the book of Yehoshua contain only town names, mysteries from the roots of the Oral Torah are concealed within it, for it is the first book after the Torah of Moshe.
records.targetHebrew: דְּהָאֲחִיזָה בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁבָּהּ הוּא הַגִּילּוּי דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הַמּוּשָּׂג לַלְּבָבוֹת וְנַפְשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כִּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא הוֹפָעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹרוֹ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּשְׁעַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּנַעֲשׂוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה ״חֵרוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע״ וְאָז הָיָה דַּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְבַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים] דְּאִלְמָלֵא חָטְאוּ לֹא נִיתְּנָה לָהֶם אֶלָּא הַתּוֹרָה וְסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — עֶרְכָּהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּהַתּוֹרָה הוּא מִצַּד הַזְּמַן וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ וְנִיתְּנָה בַּמִּדְבָּר, דִּקְבִיעוּת הַמָּקוֹם הוּא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ בְּסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, וּבֵיאַרְתִּי זֶה בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת מוּבָן הַכֹּל מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְבַד, כִּי הָיָה גָּלוּי אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתּוֹרָה הַמֵּאִיר וּמְגַלֶּה כָּל נֶעֱלָם אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא נֶעֱלַם זֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּעֱלַם הָאוֹר דְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית שֶׁנִּגְנַז לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁנִּגְנַז בַּתּוֹרָה וְהַהִתְגַּלּוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא תִּיקּוּן הַחֵטְא, כִּי ״הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע״ וְלֹא עַל לְהַבָּא לְבַד, רַק גַּם עַל מַה שֶּׁעָבַר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל בְּתִיקּוּן הָעֲבֵירוֹת ״לְהוֹסִיף בְּלִימּוּד״, וּבָזֶה נִתְבַּטֵּל הַיֵּצֶר וּכְפִי הָהַעֲמָקָה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כָּךְ יוּכַל לְהַשִּׂיג מֵעִמְקֵי מַדְרֵיגַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַיְגִיעָה בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה לְהַשִּׂיג מֵעִמְקֵי הַתּוֹרָה, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּלֶּה לוֹ כָּל אוֹרוֹת הַתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת מְאִירִים לוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא נִדְחֶה כָּל מִינֵי חֲשֵׁכוֹת וְעַל כֵּן בִּשְׁלֵימוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִשְׁלַם כָּל תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם, וְנִתְגַּלָּה אוֹר הַבָּהִיר שֶׁבִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּאֲחִידָא בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וּבְעֵץ הַחַיִּים
records.targetEnglish: Holding fast to Torah is possible only through the Oral Torah, in which the Written Torah is revealed in a way accessible to the hearts and souls of Israel. The Written Torah cannot be apprehended except through the Oral Torah. For the Written Torah was God’s manifestation of His light to Israel at the giving of the Torah, through which they became free of the evil inclination. At that time the Written Torah alone would have sufficed, as stated in Nedarim: had they not sinned, they would have been given only the Torah and the book of Yehoshua, the arrangement of the Land of Israel. The Torah concerns time and the soul and was given in the wilderness; the fixing of place is set forth in Yehoshua. I have explained this elsewhere. In any event, everything could have been understood from the Written Torah alone, because God’s light within the Torah, which illuminates and reveals every concealed thing, was manifest. Through sin this became concealed, just as the light of the six days of creation was hidden away for the righteous in the future, and the Sages said that it was hidden within the Torah. Its disclosure comes through the Oral Torah, which repairs sin, for Torah is a remedy for the evil inclination—not only concerning the future, but also what has already passed. Thus the Sages said that repairing transgressions requires increasing one’s study; through this the inclination is subdued. According to the depth of one’s Torah study, one can attain the depths of repentance that repair what came before. Through labor in the Oral Torah to attain the Torah’s depths, all its lights are revealed and shine for the person, and every kind of darkness is consequently driven away. Therefore, with the completion of the Oral Torah, the repair of all that came before is completed, and the clear light within Israel is revealed, holding fast to Torah and the Tree of Life.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains why the same passage can say that everything was already contained in the Torah and nevertheless require later Oral Torah labor. Sin conceals the received light; study both discloses it and repairs the obstruction. Its distinction between Torah’s account of time and soul and Yehoshua’s account of place clarifies the special role of the Land’s arrangement in Pri Tzadik’s argument. The completion described is the outcome of sustained study and repentance, rather than an excuse for the sin that created concealment.

records.themeTitle: Two methods carry the Torah’s hidden depth
records.themeSummary: The gentler Torah of the Land of Israel and Babylonia’s sharper inquiry have distinct strengths within the Oral Torah.
records.originHebrew: וּבֶאֱמֶת בְּלִשְׁכַּת הַגָּזִית שֶׁמִּשָּׁם יָצָא הוֹרָאָה לֹא הָיָה מַחֲלוֹקֶת רַק אַחַר כָּךְ בְּבָבֶל הִתְחִיל עִיקָר הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת וּמִלְחֲמוֹת הַשֵּׁם שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה. וְכֵן נִדְרָשׁ (סַנְהֶדְרִין כד.) יִצְהָר אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנּוֹחִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה כְּשֶׁמֶן זַיִת וּשְׁנַיִם זֵתִים עָלֶיהָ אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁמְּרִירִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה כַּזַּיִת. וְזֶהוּ בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף וְדָוִד יוֹסֵף נִקְרָא זַיִת עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר זַיִת רַעֲנָן יְפֵה פְרִי תֹאַר שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף שֶׁנִּקְרָא יְפֵה תוֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה עַל שֵׁם שֶׁגּוּפוֹ נָקִי וּמְהוּדָּר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מַאֲמָר כא) וְדָוִד יִצְהָר שֶׁנּוֹחִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה. וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ (שָׁם) נוֹעַם אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁמַּנְעִימִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה חוֹבְלִים אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁמְּחַבְּלִים זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה. וְהַיְינוּ דְּעִיקָר שׁוֹרֶשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ. וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַפִּלְפּוּל וְהַמִּלְחָמָה בְּבָבֶל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוּכָּה מד.) דִּלְכוֹן אֲמַרִי דִּלְהוֹן הִיא וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (שָׁם כ.) עֶזְרָא מִבָּבֶל וְיִסְּדָהּ כּוּלֵּי הִלֵּל הַבַּבְלִי וְיִסְּדָהּ כּוּלֵּי עָלוּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּבָנָיו וְיִסְּדוּהָ.
records.originEnglish: In truth, in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which authoritative instruction went forth, there was no dispute. Only afterward, in Babylonia, did the principal arena of disagreement and the wars of Hashem within the Oral Torah begin. Thus the Sages expound (Sanhedrin 24a): “‘Oil’ refers to the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel, who are gentle with one another in halakhic discussion, like olive oil.” “‘And two olive trees beside it’ refers to the Torah scholars of Babylonia, who are bitter toward one another in halakhic discussion, like an olive.” These are the aspects of Yosef and David. Yosef is called an olive, in keeping with the verse “A flourishing olive tree, beautiful with shapely fruit.” This is the aspect of Yosef, who is called “beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance,” because his body is pure and adorned with holiness, as explained in discourse 21. David corresponds to oil: being gentle with one another in halakhic discussion. Likewise, they expounded there: “‘Pleasantness’ refers to the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel, who are pleasant with one another in halakhic discussion.” “‘Wounders’ refers to the Torah scholars of Babylonia, who wound one another through sharp contention in halakhic discussion.” The principal root of the Oral Torah is in the Land of Israel, as we have explained. Nevertheless, its incisive reasoning and battle are in Babylonia, as stated (Sukkah 44a), “I thought the Torah was yours, but it is theirs, the Babylonians’.” Likewise, the Sages said (there, 20a): “Ezra came up from Babylonia and established it,” and so forth; “Hillel the Babylonian established it,” and so forth; “Rabbi Chiya and his sons came up and established it.”
records.targetHebrew: וְאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַתְרָא (קמ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳): דְּזוֹ מִשְׁנָה אוֹ תַּלְמוּד, עַיֵּן שָׁם, דְּנִרְאֶה דְּתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּ"סִינַי" וְ"עוֹקֵר הָרִים" אֵיזֶה עָדִיף בְּסוֹף הוֹרָיוֹת (י״ד עַמּוּד א׳): דִּסְתָם שִׁלּוּחַ "סִינַי עָדִיף", שֶׁזֶּהוּ דֶּרֶךְ לִמּוּד בְּנֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנּוֹחִים זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה [סַנְהֶדְרִין כ״ד עַמּוּד א׳], וְרַבִּי זֵירָא יָתֵיב מְאָה תַעֲנִיָּתָא דְּלִישְׁתַּכַּח מִנֵּיהּ תַּלְמוּדָא דְּבַבְלָאָה כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בָּבָא מְצִיעָא (פ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳), עַל כֵּן הוּא אָמַר הָעֲדִיפוּת לַמִּשְׁנָה; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן רָבָא, דְּהוּא הָיָה מֵרָאשֵׁי הַמְפַלְפְּלִים מְיַסְּדֵי הַתַּלְמוּד בַּבְלִי, כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: הֲוָיוֹת דְּאַבַּיֵי וְרָבָא [סֻכָּה כ״ח עַמּוּד א׳], עַל כֵּן אָמַר אִיפְּכָא; וְתַרְוַיְיהוּ "יֵין מָסָכְתִּי" הָרוֹמֵז לְמַסֶּכְתּוֹת הַמִּשְׁנָה וְתַלְמוּד, וְשָׁם גָּנוּז גַּם כֵּן כָּל סוֹדוֹת הַתּוֹרָה בְּהֶעְלֵם כַּיָּדוּעַ.
records.targetEnglish: In Bava Batra 145b the Sages interpret “a cheerful heart has a continual feast” as referring either to Mishnah or to Talmud; see there. It appears that this depends upon the disagreement at the end of Horayot, 14a, over which is preferable: “Sinai” comprehensive received knowledge or “an uprooter of mountains” exceptional analytical power. The answer sent without qualification was that Sinai takes precedence. This is the manner of study of the people of the Land of Israel, who are gentle with one another in halakhic discussion. Rabbi Zeira undertook a hundred fasts so that the Babylonian Talmud would be forgotten by him, as stated at the end of Bava Metzia 85a; he therefore assigned the advantage to Mishnah. Rava, by contrast, was among the leading practitioners of incisive reasoning who established the Babylonian Talmud, as in “the discussions of Abaye and Rava.” He therefore said the reverse. Both are “the wine I have mixed,” alluding to the tractates of Mishnah and Talmud; within them all the Torah’s secrets are also hidden, as is known.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim supplies a second, concrete account of the two study traditions: comprehensive received knowledge and the analytical work that uproots difficulties. It preserves the differing judgments of Rabbi Zeira and Rava while locating hidden Torah depth in both. This illuminates why Pri Tzadik can acknowledge the Land of Israel as the principal root and still give Babylonia’s reasoning an indispensable role, without making the two methods identical.

records.themeTitle: The covenant is inscribed beyond present awareness
records.themeSummary: The “statutes of Your will” disclose an enduring divine bond, illustrated by circumcision before the infant can knowingly choose.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁעָמְדוּ עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל לְהַעֲבִירָם מֵחֻקֵּי רְצוֹנֶךָ. וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּסְּפָרִים שֶׁגְּזֵירַת הַיְּוָנִים הָיָה לְבַטֵּל מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל חוֹדֶשׁ שַׁבָּת וּמִילָה וְהֵם נִקְרְאוּ חוּקֵּי רְצוֹנֶךָ שֶׁנֶּחְקַק בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהֵם קְשׁוּרִים בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה דְּאִיקְרֵי רָצוֹן. שַׁבָּת קְדוּשָׁה קְבִיעָא וְקַיְּימָא דִּכְתִיב לָדַעַת כִּי אֲנִי הַשֵּׁם מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם וְנֶחְקַק הַקְּדוּשָׁה בַּלֵּב לְהַשְׁאִיר לְשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים בְּהַבְדָּלָה בַּתְּפִלָּה וַתְּלַמְּדֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת חֻקֵּי רְצוֹנֶךָ. וְחוֹדֶשׁ גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְּדוּשַׁת עַתִּיקָא וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג עט ב) אוּף הָכִי בְּחַדְתּוּתֵי סִיהֲרָא דְּהָא נָהִיר לָהּ שִׁמְשָׁא בְּחֶדְוָותָא דִּנְהִירוּ דְּעַתִּיקָא. וְכֵן מִילָה שֶׁנִּימּוֹל תִּינוֹק לְח׳ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ וְנַעֲשֶׂה יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶה מוֹרֶה שֶׁנּוֹלַד בִּקְדוּשַׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁקָּשׁוּר בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ בָּרָצוֹן הָעֶלְיוֹן
records.originEnglish: as we have explained: the Greeks rose against Israel “to turn them away from the statutes of Your will.” This follows what is written in the books: the Greeks decreed the abolition among Israel of the New Moon, Shabbat, and circumcision. These are called “the statutes of Your will,” because God’s will is engraved in Israel’s heart. They are bound at their root to the beginning of divine thought, which is called Will. Shabbat’s holiness is fixed and enduring, as it is written, “To know that I am Hashem who sanctifies you.” That holiness is engraved in the heart so that it remains for the six working days, as we say in the Havdalah passage of the Amidah, “You taught us to perform the statutes of Your will.” The New Moon also contains something of the holiness of Atika, the Ancient One. As stated in Zohar III, 79b: “So, too, at the renewal of the moon, for the sun shines upon it with the joy of the radiance of the Ancient One.” Likewise, an infant is circumcised on the eighth day without his own awareness and becomes marked in the covenant as an Israelite. This shows that he was born with Israel’s holiness, bound at his root to the supernal Will.
records.targetHebrew: ובכל זאת האיר השי"ת לנו הארת שם הוי' עד שנתברר אפילו הלבוש אחרון של ישראל ועל זה הבירור רומז הארת שם הוי' שאף הגוף הגשמי של ישראל הוא מלא דברי תורה גם בלא דעתם וכמאמרם ז"ל ליהודים היתה אורה ושמחה וששון וכו' ששון זו מילה ומילה רומז שנחקק בהגוף הגשמי דברי תורה ע"ד שנאמר לא כברית אשר וגו' ואתם הפרתם את בריתי אלא ועל לבם אכתבנו וגו' היינו כי זאת המצוה מקיף את האדם גם בשעת שינה ואף בבית המרחץ כדאיתא (מנחות מג: ובמדרש ש"ט ו) בשעה שנכנס דוד לבית המרחץ וכו' וכיון שנזכר במילה שבבשרו נתיישבה דעתו וכו':
records.targetEnglish: Despite all this the extreme concealment at the time of Purim, God illuminated for us the radiance of the divine Name, until even Israel’s final garment the physical body was clarified. This clarification is indicated by the radiance of that Name: even Israel’s physical body is full of words of Torah without their conscious awareness. As the Sages said, “The Jews had light, joy, gladness,” and so forth: “Gladness” is circumcision. Circumcision signifies that words of Torah are engraved in the physical body, as expressed in the saying, “Not like the covenant which…” and “you broke My covenant,” but rather, “I shall write it upon their hearts.” This commandment surrounds the person even during sleep and even in the bathhouse. Thus Menachot 43 and Midrash Shocher Tov 6 relate that when David entered the bathhouse, and so forth, once he remembered the circumcision in his flesh, his mind was put at ease.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains how a covenantal bond can be real before, and beyond, the person’s present awareness: its sign remains engraved in the body when no conscious act is being performed. This sharpens Pri Tzadik’s use of the infant’s circumcision to disclose a holiness rooted in divine will. The target develops the point through Purim and David’s bathhouse experience; it is a conceptual explanation of the enduring bond, not an identification of the festivals’ laws.

records.themeSummary: Pri Tzadik proposes that the first sight of the miracle prompted an additional lighting as an expression of joy.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ נִרְאֶה דְּקָאֵי עַל נֵרוֹת חֲנוּכָּה שֶׁתֵּיכֶף בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן כְּשֶׁרָאוּ הַנֵּס שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּיֵּיר הַשֶּׁמֶן בַּפַּךְ אוֹ שֶׁהֵאִיר אוֹר גָּדוֹל עַל פִּי נֵס אַף שֶׁעָשׂוּ פְּתִילוֹת דַּקּוֹת מְאֹד וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ לְתֵירוּץ הַבֵּית יוֹסֵף אָז מֵחֲמַת שִׂמְחָה הִדְלִיקוּ נֵרוֹת. שֶׁהָיָה אָז גַּם כֵּן מִנְהָג לְהַדְלִיק נֵרוֹת מֵחֲמַת שִׂמְחָה
records.originEnglish: It appears, however, to refer to Chanukah lights. Immediately on the first day, when they saw the miracle—that the oil remained in the flask, or that a great light shone miraculously although they had made very thin wicks, as we explained in applying the Beit Yosef’s answer—they kindled lights out of joy. Lighting lamps as an expression of joy was a custom in those times as well,

records.targetEnglish: The Gemara, Sukkah 51, says: “One who has not seen the rejoicing at the place of the water drawing has never seen rejoicing in his life,” and, “There was no courtyard in Jerusalem that was not illuminated by the light of the place of the water drawing.” The pious and people of good deeds would dance before them with flaming torches. The principal joy of this celebration came from the light with which God showed them that their connection to Him had never ceased. In truth, from God’s side nothing is devoid of His glory; only from the human perspective does there sometimes appear to be, Heaven forbid, a void and interruption between the person and the light of His glory. On this festival God illuminated their own perception as well, so that they explicitly recognized, even retrospectively, their connection to the light of His will. This illumination gave rise to their great joy.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the inner cause of a celebration expressed through abundant light: a previously obscured relation to God becomes perceptible. This adds depth to Pri Tzadik’s proposal that joy at the revealed miracle itself prompted lighting. The target concerns Sukkot’s water-drawing celebration; the comparison explains the relation between disclosure, joy, and light, and does not supply historical evidence for the Chanukah custom.
